extracted.intended_audience: empirical education economists, applied microeconometricians, and policy researchers studying peer effects in school settings
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and empirical standards for identifying and estimating peer effects for primary-school students using class-within-school variation in survey data (PIRLS), including measurement error correction, tests of random assignment, construction of peer measures, and robustness checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Within-school identification / random formation of classes
rubrics_metrics.description: “The identification relies on variation across classes within schools. We argue that classes within primary schools are formed roughly randomly with respect to family background.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use within-school (school fixed-effect) comparisons to break the correlation between peer composition and class-level shocks. Demonstrate plausibility by testing whether class assignment is (approximately) random conditional on school; if systematic within-school sorting exists (e.g., Sweden, immigrant clustering), interpret within-school estimates with caution or perform sensitivity checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estimate reduced-form peer effect (address reflection problem)
rubrics_metrics.description: Because of the Manski reflection problem it is difficult to separate endogenous (φ) and exogenous (δ) peer effects, so the paper follows the literature in estimating the reduced-form parameter λ on peers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly state that the estimate λ captures either endogenous or exogenous effects (or both). Use reduced-form estimates for policy-relevant conclusions while acknowledging the inability to disentangle the two without strong restrictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control for school fixed effects / school-level peer means
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimate y_ics with α_s (a set of dummy variables for each school) or include school-level peer variables to remove bias from correlated (school-level) effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare specifications with school fixed effects, school peer means, and between-school models. Large differences signal selection at the school level or omitted correlated effects; report and discuss such differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction of peer variables: leave-out classroom means
rubrics_metrics.description: “The peer variable for student i used in the regressions is the leave-out mean for the classroom, omitting the value of the variable for student i from the calculation of the mean.” Peer averages are formed for five background variables: number of books at home, sex, age, whether a parent was born abroad, and whether a foreign language is spoken at home.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form leave-out class averages to avoid mechanical correlation with the individual's own value. When forming class averages, use all students who report the specific variable (not only the analytic sample) to reduce sampling noise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use alternative operationalizations of peer quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Number of books at home can be used either as a 1–5 index or as fractions in the five categories; alternative peer measures (e.g., parents' education index) should be tried.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report results for multiple peer constructions (index vs category fractions; alternative background indices) and check robustness of sign, magnitude, and significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test random assignment to classes via Pearson Chi² tests
rubrics_metrics.description: To test whether classrooms are formed randomly with respect to a student characteristic, perform Pearson Chi² tests within each school and aggregate p-values (sum of school test statistics).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute school-specific χ2 p-values and plot their distribution (uniform under random assignment). Interpret left/right skew—left skew indicates deliberate balancing, right skew indicates clustering. Use Monte Carlo to assess test size in finite samples and be cautious when sample sizes are small.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test whether class composition correlates with resources
rubrics_metrics.description: Run regressions of peer variables on class, teacher, and school characteristics (class size, teacher gender/education/experience, town size, instruction hours, shortages of staff/materials/rooms) and report F-tests for joint significance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If class composition predicts observable classroom or resource characteristics, correlated effects may bias peer estimates; examine both class-level and school-level variables, and present results with and without school fixed effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require sufficient within-school variance in peer composition
rubrics_metrics.description: “A necessary condition for the within school estimation to work is... that there is sufficient variance in peer composition of a classroom within a school.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present variance decomposition (within vs between schools) for peer measures and test scores; if within-school variance is negligible, within-school identification will be weak or infeasible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for survey sampling design and plausible values
rubrics_metrics.description: PIRLS uses a two-stage stratified sampling design (schools chosen as primary sampling units, then classes), and reading scores are reported as plausible values drawn from an estimated proficiency distribution and standardized to international mean=500, SD=100.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge the sampling design in estimation/variance calculation and use plausible values appropriately (combine estimates across plausible values or follow recommended procedures). Note that schools are primary sampling units; consider clustering/weights as required by design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handle missing data and item nonresponse transparently
rubrics_metrics.description: Missing values (e.g., parents' education missing 36%) require alternative variables (number of books used because of better response) or missing-data strategies; authors also report replacing missing by zeros plus missing dummies and compare results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report how missingness is handled (drop, impute, missing dummies) and test sensitivity. Prefer background variables with higher response rates when possible; show that alternative treatments produce comparable peer estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correct for measurement error and sampling error in peer variables
rubrics_metrics.description: Because peer measures are self-reported by parents and the sample may not include all students in a classroom, measurement error and sampling error bias OLS and within-school estimates; use instruments/adjustments to correct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model classical measurement error and sampling variability explicitly (appendix derivations). Use independent measurements or IV strategies to correct attenuation and other biases; explain how incomplete sampling within classes inflates measurement error and how leave-out means and IV mitigate it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instrumental variables using independent measurements
rubrics_metrics.description: Use instruments based on independent measurements (z1_ics, z2_cs) and show conditions for consistency (appendix derivations). IV can recover consistent peer coefficients under specific variance conditions (e.g., var components).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present instrument construction, justify independence of measurement errors, and report IV results alongside OLS; discuss assumptions required for IV consistency and perform sensitivity checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report OLS vs within-school vs IV comparisons
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare standard OLS (between-school) estimates to within-school (school fixed effects) and measurement-error-corrected (IV) estimates; differences inform roles of selection and measurement error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If within-school coefficients shrink versus OLS, interpret as school selection or measurement error; if measurement-error-corrected within-school estimates approach OLS, emphasize the role of measurement error rather than selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude schools with reported ability grouping (tracking) in robustness checks
rubrics_metrics.description: Some schools report forming classes on the basis of ability (notably France and the Netherlands); results should be shown excluding these schools.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Run robustness checks excluding schools that report ability grouping/tracking and report whether peer coefficients change materially.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret the distribution of p-values and clustering for immigrant students
rubrics_metrics.description: Histograms of school-specific p-values indicate roughly random assignment on family background and sex, but clustering (low p-values) for immigrant and non-native language students.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate and report subgroup non-randomness (e.g., immigrant clustering) and show how this affects peer estimates (e.g., analyze immigrant-related peer measures separately or control for correlated resources).

rubrics_metrics.name: Include rich student/class/school covariates
rubrics_metrics.description: Control variables include gender, age, immigrant status, language at home, household size, number of books (individual level), class size and squared, teacher’s sex, education, experience and squared, and school characteristics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report specifications with student-level controls only, with added class/school covariates, and with school fixed effects to show robustness; document whether adding covariates materially changes peer estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variance decomposition of peer measures into within- and between-school components
rubrics_metrics.description: Decompose total variance of class averages into within- and between-school components using relationship (6). Table 3 presents total, between and within school variance of peer variables.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present variance decomposition to quantify how much peer variation is exploitable by within-school estimation; use weighting appropriate for unbalanced panels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convert estimated peer effects to standardized effect sizes and compare literature
rubrics_metrics.description: Convert estimated coefficients into effect sizes (e.g., SD change in reading per SD change in peer composition) and compare with previous studies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report effect sizes with confidence intervals and situate estimates relative to the range of findings in the literature (from near zero to large). Highlight uncertainty (wide CIs) where applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Monte Carlo/simulation checks for small-sample behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors performed a small Monte Carlo experiment showing the Pearson Chi² test tends to reject too often under the null for samples of their size.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where small-sample bias is suspected, use simulation to check test size and power; interpret p-values and test outcomes in light of finite-sample performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report caveats: measurement error importance, selection limited, imprecision
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors note: “Our results suggest that the peer effect is modestly large, measurement error is important in our survey data, and selection plays little role in biasing peer effects estimates. We find no significant evidence of non-linear peer effects.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about limitations: potential remaining measurement error, clustering of specific subgroups (immigrants), large confidence intervals for corrected estimates, and the generalizability from sampled countries/cohorts.
